profile.campus_mw_context: The 128,715-sq. ft. data center in Sterling, VA, offers 11 MW of IT capacity and features robust connectivity options with high bandwidth and high-availability circuits and a number of metro and long-haul networks.

reading.body:
CyrusOne NVA4 in Sterling offers 11 MW of IT capacity across 128,715 square feet, which translates to roughly 275 racks assuming 40 kW per rack, a common density for AI training hardware.

The facility emphasizes network connectivity with multiple metro and long-haul circuits available. This architectural choice addresses data movement constraints for distributed training workloads, where bottlenecks in inter-rack communication can degrade performance as severely as compute shortages. Virginia has 330 mapped data centers, but only 25 publish capacity figures totaling 1,603 MW. This campus ranks 26th among Virginia facilities with disclosed capacity, representing less than 1% of the state's published total. Whether this matters depends on what remains hidden: 305 Virginia facilities have no published capacity, and their aggregate power may exceed the disclosed figures substantially.

The facility's modest scale and lack of published power credentials beyond IT load mean it is unlikely to host large-scale training runs or frontier model development. It is positioned for enterprise workloads, specialized compute, or distributed inference where network quality substitutes for raw power density. The proximity to Washington Dulles airport and dense metro networks makes it suitable for latency-sensitive applications, but this is orthogonal to the constraint that binds AI scaling: absolute power availability. Without visibility into Virginia's unmapped facilities, this single site tells little about the state's true role in AI infrastructure growth.
